cells.tense: You are bearing what has to be borne, and the bearing is not costing you yourself.
cells.ask: Name one load you're carrying well and let it keep its shape tonight; catch your hand before it loosens or tightens a thing that's holding fine on its own.
cells.core:
Something you were braced against has come down — a structure, an arrangement, an assumption about how it had to go — and you're in the open space it left, carrying what's actually yours. You hold what's real, and you let what just proved false stay down instead of shoring it back up.

Some days a grip will close hard and you'll notice it, and from the outside it looks like strength. So the practice is small, and now while it's easy: pick one weight you're carrying well, say out loud that you're carrying it, and leave it the size it is tonight. Don't loosen it and don't tighten it. The hand that knows it's choosing — that's the one to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying what's real, and you know you're carrying it.

cells.tense: You are going to hold it whether or not it falls, and the bracing has already started.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're watching to hold together and let it run out of your hands for a day; when the fixes start in your head, name one trade you can actually keep.
cells.core:
Nothing has dropped yet, and you're already gripping. The brace runs ahead of the fall — you've checked it twice, you've got the recovery ready, and some of what you're carrying on that schedule isn't even yours. The grip has started doing the opposite of its job. Held that tight, things stop being able to move.

But there is a way back. Fairness, in the plain sense of the word: what's actually yours to hold, and what isn't. One thing you're watching at all hours — let it run for a day without your hand on it. When the fixing starts up in your head, ask what your share really is, then dial one thing until your share and your grip line up. That's maintenance, not defeat.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for a fall that hasn't started.

cells.tense: You stopped reaching for the things that hold people up long before now.
cells.ask: Take your hands off one thing that's already finished and leave them off for a day; let one person keep a hand on something you're holding.
cells.core:
Ask directly for what holds a person up and it goes heavy in your mouth. So you've stopped asking. You stand close to what you need and don't reach for it — under pressure the body goes quiet at the edge instead. You can't steady yourself if you won't use something outside your own arms, holding feels dangerous.

Strength is still available to you and it isn't about hardness. Let one finished thing go — take your hands off it and leave them off. And let one person keep a hand on something you're holding, even if you could hold it alone. Then the actual lifting — yours and theirs — keeps its size, and stays visible.
cells.sheetLine: Holding on is easy for you. Being held is not.

cells.tense: A strength in you is holding steady while you tell the room it's nothing much.
cells.ask: Say out loud that you carried one hard week, then write one plain sentence about what kept something steady while it was hard.
cells.core:
Some part of you holds while the rest of you looks somewhere else. You carried a stretch that would have flattened people and filed it under getting through. That holding is running right now and you're not claiming it. What you don't see isn't that you're worn out — it's that you have something holding.

So name it once. Notice one thing you stayed steady through — a week, a bad stretch, a decision nobody watched you make — then say plainly that you carried it. What you say about the strength is part of what builds it. Keep the evidence small and let it stand.
cells.sheetLine: You're steady in ways you haven't given yourself credit for.
